planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Dark Knight is one of the most widely planted caryopteris cultivars, valued for its especially deep flower color.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Dark Knight is drought-tolerant once established and, like other caryopteris, dies back to the ground in cold winters, resprouting from the base each spring. Aromatic, gray-green foliage sets off dense clusters of deep violet-blue, fringed flowers that wreathe the upper stems from late summer into fall, one of the darkest and richest flower colors among widely available caryopteris cultivars, providing valuable late-season nectar for bees and butterflies when many other shrubs have finished flowering. It is a compact, easy-care choice for the front or middle of a sunny border, tolerating heat, drought, and poor soil once established. Cut the whole plant back to a few inches from the ground in late winter, since it flowers on new wood and benefits from hard annual pruning to stay compact and floriferous.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Worcester Gold is grown as much for its golden foliage as for its flowers.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Worcester Gold is drought-tolerant once established and, like other caryopteris, dies back to the ground in cold winters, resprouting from the base each spring. Its aromatic foliage emerges bright golden-yellow and holds much of that color through the season, providing a season-long foliage accent that most other caryopteris cultivars lack, and in late summer the plant adds clusters of blue, fringed flowers that contrast attractively against the gold leaves. It is a compact, easy-care choice for the front or middle of a sunny border, tolerating heat, drought, and poor soil once established, though a little afternoon shade helps prevent leaf scorch on the palest gold foliage in the hottest climates. Cut the whole plant back to a few inches from the ground in late winter, since it flowers on new wood and benefits from hard annual pruning to stay compact and floriferous.

common_name: First Choice Bluebeard (Compact Deep Blue Caryopteris)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; First Choice is a compact cultivar with darker green foliage than most caryopteris.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; First Choice is drought-tolerant once established and, like other caryopteris, dies back to the ground in cold winters, resprouting from the base each spring. It bears darker, glossier green foliage than most caryopteris cultivars, which are typically gray-green, providing a richer backdrop for the dense clusters of deep blue, fringed flowers that wreathe the upper stems from late summer into fall. Its naturally compact, rounded habit fits neatly into a smaller sunny border or foundation planting without the sprawl of larger cultivars, and it provides valuable late-season nectar for bees and butterflies. Cut the whole plant back to a few inches from the ground in late winter, since it flowers on new wood and benefits from hard annual pruning to stay compact and floriferous.

common_name: Sunshine Blue Bluebeard (Compact Golden Foliage Caryopteris)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Sunshine Blue combines bright gold foliage with a compact habit better suited to holding its color through summer heat than some older gold-leaved caryopteris.

directions: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in average to lean, well-drained soil in full sun; Sunshine Blue is drought-tolerant once established and, like other caryopteris, dies back to the ground in cold winters, resprouting from the base each spring. Its bright golden-yellow foliage holds color well through the growing season on a compact, rounded plant, providing a season-long foliage accent in addition to the clusters of blue, fringed flowers that wreathe the upper stems from late summer into fall. The combination of gold foliage and blue flowers gives strong two-tone contrast in a sunny border, and it provides valuable late-season nectar for bees and butterflies. A little afternoon shade in the hottest climates helps prevent leaf scorch on the palest gold foliage. Cut the whole plant back to a few inches from the ground in late winter, since it flowers on new wood and benefits from hard annual pruning to stay compact and floriferous.
